items.title: First Liberty: Minnesota County Has ‘Essentially Criminalized Being Amish’
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: Wow.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

The Amish community in Minnesota is pushing back amid claims of unfair government policies that purportedly fail to offer religious accommodations — and even reportedly led to one Amish man’s arrest.

First Liberty attorney Ryan Gardner said his firm is representing two Amish congregations in Mille Lacs County, Minnesota, arguing the county itself has “essentially criminalized being Amish.”

“As you might know, the Amish community lives by a pretty strict set of religious principles, and many of those involve not being involved in technology,” Gardner said. “And kind of keeping to themselves … they want to be able to live according to their religious beliefs, and a lot of what those beliefs require, frankly … to be set apart from modern society.”

According to First Liberty, problems began for these congregations during COVID-19, when county officials reportedly implemented a new permitting system for building structures and homes.

“It went from a paper form to an electronic form,” Gardner said. “As you might imagine, the Amish don’t really use electronic forms or the internet, so this was a significant problem, and they had no alternative for a long time.”

With no other option for simply getting clearance to build homes, he said “a lot of the people in these congregations just proceeded to build anyways because they didn’t have a choice.”

Gardner said Mille Lacs County did eventually change the policy to make a paper option available, but added there is an additional $50 fee for requesting permitting on paper.

“Pretty much the only people who are actually using that are the Amish, and so now they’re having to pay a special fee just to even start the permitting process,” the lawyer said. “And once they get in, there are more problems because they’re trying to impose all kinds of modern requirements that are just inconsistent with the Amish way of life.”

Gardner said officials have been so hard on the Amish that they even put one man in jail “for the crime of building and living in his home.”

“This particular individual had been living in his home for something like five years and then, suddenly, he’s criminally cited for it, and he goes to court, and he’s convicted,” the lawyer said. “And he is … immediately taken to jail.”

Gardner said it is “ludicrous” and “extreme” to prosecute someone for such a “petty” offense, and added that such a reaction is rare. He added that the Amish had purportedly tried to go to the county to work the issue out but were “met with hostility.”

“Here’s the kicker in all of this,” he continued, “Built into the very ordinance that the county is enforcing here is a provision that gives the county discretion to give exemptions to these requirements to anybody that it wants.”

First Liberty sent a letter to the county recently demanding they stop enforcement actions against the Amish, especially considering warrants that are currently out for others. They’re also looking for an exemption that would settle the issue once and for all, noting that, from his perspective, the Amish build insanely safe structures.

Mille Lacs County told CBN News that lawyers cannot comment on ongoing cases.

items.title: 9/11 Survivor’s Chilling Warning About ‘Evil’ 25 Years Later
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: Wow.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

A former Secret Service agent who survived the Sept. 11 terror attacks is warning that he believes some Americans might not be gleaning important lessons from the deadly assault.

Darin Kinder said he “had a front row seat to evil” that fateful day, but that he also “saw the best of America” amid the terror.

“I was outside when the second impact happened 80-90 yards from the base of that tower,” he said. “And then scurried up into World Trade Tower OneIwith some other coworkers, helping people evacuate.”

Then, he was at the base of Tower Two when it buckled and collapsed. It was in that moment that Kinder faced a harrowing situation, as he was in a battle for his life.

“That began my mad dash for life,” he said. “That’s when I thought it was gone for sure. I thought it was game over.”

Kinder tried to outrun the tower’s collapse, struggling to breathe through the thick smoke. He was able to survive and flee the chaos and has spent the past 25 years sharing his story. His memoir, “Bury Me in a Dirty Suit: Discovering Man’s Valiant Purpose in the Aftermath Of 9/11,” has been one of the tools he has used to offer up his journey toward hope and healing.

Among the other topics he covered is courage, something he described as “a choice.” And as Kinder reflects on the hope he experienced amid so much pain, he also has a warning for Americans 25 years after radical Islam inflicted such pain on the nation: that some might have forgotten what unfolded.

“I think a September 10th mindset is kind of encroaching in, and where we just want to keep our head buried in the sand and not address the real evil that’s there, the real presence of a threat that’s there,” Kinder said. “And we can’t have that.”

He said he’s been bothered and concerned by some of what he’s seen among young people who are asking questions to which they should know the answers. Tragically, he said many of these people simply haven’t been educated on these matters, with the facts of what unfolded at the hands of “19 radical Islamic terrorists” being shielded or ignored.

Kinder also said other historic elements surrounding the event that “killed nearly 3,000 Americans and that kicked off a generational war — the global War on Terror — that we have seen the negative ripple and ramifications of” have also been largely ignored. He encouraged people to adhere to the truth, and warned that some Christians are too focused on the wrong elements.

“It’s this devout devotion to the 11th Commandment — ‘Thou shall be nice,'” Kinder said. “And it’s just not there. I mean, we’re we’re commanded to speak the truth in love and truth without love is harsh. Love without truth is just trying to be a nice guy that gets along to go-a-long. We have to be able to to to relay the truth to the next generation.”

Kinder said it’s often a temptation for Christians to want to be comfortable, yet Scripture shows Jesus and his followers weren’t always in that position. In fact, they were “hunted…chased out of town” and even beaten and stoned.

“We want to embrace comfort and not have real conversations,” he said, noting that the history of Islam was one of imposition at its roots, juxtaposing it against Christianity, which he called a “religion of invitation.” Understanding these realities, he said, is key.

“I would just say bluntly that evil doesn’t stop when you ask nicely,” he said. “And when it reaches its radical form and it’s literally attacking you physically or it’s undercutting everything in your culture and everything in your society and slowly changing over time that needs to be pushed back.”

Kinder continued, “That is darkness, and we’re called to bring light into dark.”

He encouraged Christians to “get engaged” and to stop burying their heads in the sand. Read more of his story in “Bury Me in a Dirty Suit: Discovering Man’s Valiant Purpose in the Aftermath Of 9/11.”

items.title: Khloé Kardashian Says Faith Was “the Foundation of Our Childhood”
items.author: RELEVANT Staff
items.summary: The Kardashians have spent nearly two decades documenting just about every corner of family life (even the manufactured ones). But apparently, that also includes matching church outfits and nightly prayers. In a clip from her podcast, Khloé in Wonder Land, posted Sunday, Khloé Kardashian opened up a
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

The Kardashians have spent nearly two decades documenting just about every corner of family life (even the manufactured ones). But apparently, that also includes matching church outfits and nightly prayers.

In a clip from her podcast, Khloé in Wonder Land, posted Sunday, Khloé Kardashian opened up about the faith she and her siblings grew up with. The clip comes from her December 2025 episode “Why I Believe: Khloé on Faith.”

“My parents are both Christians,” she said. “We went to Bible study every single Sunday, got dressed up. Me and my sisters and my brother, we all matched. The hair was all done. It was what we did every Sunday, and then we would always come home and have little gatherings at our house. It was the best.”

And church wasn’t the extent of it.

“My dad prayed with us every single night like clockwork,” Kardashian said. “I don’t remember a day that he did not.”

Her father, Robert Kardashian, who died in 2003, also used to leave notes for her younger brother, Rob, before heading to work each morning.

“My dad would leave my brother notes about God every morning when my dad went to leave for work, and he would leave them in my brother’s bathroom,” she said. “Either it would be a Bible verse or something about God.”

Kourtney eventually gathered the notes for one of Rob’s birthdays and had them framed together.

“It’s hanging on his wall,” Khloé said. “It’s so beautiful, and it’s all in my dad’s handwriting.”

For Kardashian, those memories aren’t incidental family traditions. They’re how she explains the role faith played in the household.

“Faith, praying, praying over your food, praying every night — that was just the foundation of our childhood,” she said.

items.title: The Unlikely Conversion of Carlos Lehder, the Medellín Cartel’s Last‑Standing Narco
items.author: Johanna Duncan
items.summary:
Johanna Duncan

The worst day of his life became the reason he is still alive and had the opportunity to do what other narcos never could: repent and ask for forgiveness.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Johanna Duncan

There is a saying in Colombia for when someone is in great debt: “He owes this life and the next one.” But when Carlos Lehder was arrested for running the largest pirate operation in history (a scene present in the American mind via the hit Netflix show, Narcos), it was determined that he owed the American government all that and a little bit more—one life sentence plus 135 years to be precise. Now, Lehder recognizes that the worst day of his life became, in many ways, the reason he is still alive and had the opportunity to do what other narcos never could: repent and ask for forgiveness. 

Decades after this historic arrest, the once-feared kingpin of the Medellín Cartel and the man who worked to bring the Nazi party to South America has turned his life around 180 degrees, and his journey is a reminder that Jesus is truly leaving the ninety-nine to seek the one lost sheep.

In the lush mountains of Colombia, right where the Andes mountains end and slowly merge into the tropics, there’s rich soil fueled by the perfect weather where almost anything you sow will grow. These are the perfect conditions for the highest quality coffee, but also for the coca leaf—the raw material for cocaine. For locals, it almost feels like an unfair tax for being gifted with such a beautiful environment. Across this natural beauty reigned the Colombian narcos and specifically, the Medellín Cartel. Named so by the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA), this organization grew coca leaves, turned them into cocaine in clandestine labs hidden across the jungles, and shipped it internationally. That last step was Carlos Lehder’s responsibility.

Carlos is a half–German, half–Colombian, self-identified black sheep in almost every circle he has run in. According to his own words, he was quite different from his siblings. In the drug world, he also differed considerably from his fellow narcos—the most famous one being one of his greatest business partners, Pablo Escobar.

Every narco (as most criminals) knew they would end up either dead or in prison, but in the specific narco world Carlos Lehder helped build, there was something even worse than those two alternatives: extradition. The Medellín Cartel bombed planes and murdered officials and politicians to avoid it. Its members had a slogan for it: “Better a grave in Colombia than a cell in the United States.” Pablo Escobar was gunned down on a Medellín rooftop in 1993. José Gonzalo Rodríguez Gacha, “El Mexicano,” died in a police raid the same year. Lehder was already gone by then; he was extradited in 1987 and locked in an American maximum-security cell, out of reach of the war that killed almost everyone with whom he built the cartel. 

His story has been told by multiple movies, documentaries, and TV shows. But now, he is telling his own story. In the preface to his 2024 memoir, Vida y muerte del cartel de Medellín (The Life and Death of The Cartel of Medellín), this now-elderly man sits down to explain how he became one of the most feared drug traffickers in history. He begins, of all places, at his own baptism days after his birth in the cathedral of Armenia, Colombia, where he was christened Carlos Enrique Lehder Rivas. It’s a strange place to start a book about cocaine, murder, and a criminal empire that drenched a whole country in blood, but I couldn’t help notice that Lehder—the co-founder of the Medellín Cartel and the first major Colombian trafficker ever extradited to the United States—recognizes the spiritual thread ever present in his life and intentionally includes it in the story as an important moment.

His story is sprinkled with details like the time he promised Our Lady of Mount Carmel, patroness of transportation, he would never steal cars again—a promise he kept even when a tempting opportunity arose. Nonetheless, he was still in the midst of building the most lucrative illegal drug routes in history. That honesty and the details about his faith life and its maturity tell the story of the transformation of his life in his own telling—a story about faith lost and eventually found. 

The Prodigal Son

Many of Colombia’s traffickers clawed their way out of genuine poverty with no path to anything else. Lehder wasn’t one of them. His father, Klaus Wilhelm Lehder, was a German engineer who came to Colombia in 1927 to build railways; his mother, Helena Rivas, came from a proper local family. They married in the Catholic Church, raised four children, and by Lehder’s own account in his memoir, they lived a very ordinary, happy, and respectable life. The Lehder children attended private Catholic schools, were raised trilingual (English, Spanish, and German), and all except Carlos completed university degrees.

But life wasn’t too perfect. As was true for many other German families, losing World War II had a huge impact on Lehder’s father, and this led to divorce. In the midst of this abundance of opportunities and the breakdown of the Lehder family, Carlos, with his insatiable ambition, told his parents he wanted to pursue the American Dream, and they supported him. At just fifteen, he transferred his studies to a New York boarding school. The initial plan was to make money in US dollars and move back to Colombia with enough cash to buy a farm and live a peaceful life. But Carlos quickly realized that there was a faster way to reach his financial goals: reselling stolen cars and dealing marijuana to hippies. By sixteen, Carlos had chosen, in his own later words, “the wrong profession” when the right one had been sitting there for the taking.

He was eventually caught and sent to the Federal Correctional Institution Danbury in Connecticut. This only skyrocketed Carlos’s criminal career and became his own sort of university degree. It just so happened that in this prison Carlos met drug mules and received his first lessons in the emerging business of cocaine. Coincidentally, he was also in prison with the lawyers involved in the Watergate scandal—G. Gordon Liddy and E. Howard Hunt, Jr., among others. According to his own account, he learned about the American legal system from them.

After his release and deportation, Lehder visited his father and admitted that he planned to continue his life of crime, to which his father reminded him that he had a strict policy of no criminals in his house, even if it meant his own son. They hugged and didn’t see each other again for many years. 

In the years that followed, Carlos Lehder bought Norman’s Cay, a private Bahamian island he turned into a cocaine transshipment hub in the late 1970s. This turned Carlos into an official pirate. From there, he managed the shipments for almost every narco. By the time of his ultimate arrest at thirty-seven years old, he had been making an estimated $300 million per year. 

When Worse Than Death Happened

At one point in the War on Drugs, Colombian and American authorities recognized that the narcos were too powerful to be held accountable in Colombian courts, so they decided to actively enforce the 1979 extradition treaty. This meant, if a narco is caught in Colombia (or anywhere else), they would immediately be brought to the United States to face trial. The narcos knew this was a real threat and fought it under the banner of Los Extraditables (“The Extraditables”), an organization led by Pablo Escobar himself. A gruesome and violent war erupted with much bloodshed. Now, it is understood that Pablo Escobar worked a deal in order to avoid extradition by betraying one of the narcos, and Carlos Lehder was the lucky one. 

Extradited in 1987, he was delivered into the maximum-security federal system and received his famous sentence of life without parole plus 135 years. He was never meant to set foot on Colombian soil again. He landed at the US Penitentiary in Marion, Illinois—one of the harshest prisons in the American system—and by his own account, spent years of his sentence in near-total isolation. It was there, cut off from the empire he’d built and the country he’d terrorized, that the second half of his story begins.

The Priest Who Ministered to Monsters

Few figures in Colombian religious life are as loved and complicated as Fr. Rafael García-Herreros. He established the Minuto de Dios (Minute for God), which started as a radio show but grew into a television show in which he preached nightly homilies to millions of Colombians and later became a non-profit assisting the poor. Fr. García-Herreros was to Colombians what Fulton Sheen was to Americans, and similarly, there’s now a beatification case opened for him. He’s already been declared a Servant of God. 

But some of his ministry was not as beloved by Colombians because somehow in the midst of his very busy work, he was, controversially, a sort of chaplain to the Medellín Cartel itself. Fr. García-Herreros baptized and offered sacraments to the narcos and their families even during the height of their reign of terror. Critics accused him of legitimizing men with blood on their hands, while supporters said he was doing what a priest is supposed to do: reaching out to sinners nobody else would go near. In 1991, it was Fr. García-Herreros who brokered Pablo Escobar’s dramatic surrender to Colombian authorities, standing beside him as cameras rolled. A year later, when Escobar escaped, Father used his television show to publicly ask Pablo Escobar to submit himself to the law.

The narcos’ faith and relationship to the Church and God himself is a tangled web of mysteries. Perhaps it is the constant proximity to death accompanied with the abundance of greed that brings about this paradox. There’s a famous story about how Pablo Escobar was almost caught multiple times because his mom refused to stop attending Mass. Undercover agents were always looking and waiting for her at churches in order to follow her in the hopes of catching her son.  

Fr. García-Herreros didn’t stop at Escobar. He travelled to visit and minister to Lehder inside the walls of the prison. While Lehder recognizes that he had turned away from God and his faith in general, he also admits that he didn’t fully stop praying in times of need and constantly sought Our Lady’s intervention. Eventually, those prayers were answered. 

In his memoir, Carlos shares that, while in prison, he recognized that for the sake of survival, he needed to completely forget about the outside world—forget about money, forget about women, forget about power, basically forget everything he had known and cherished. Once he achieved this, he encountered God. 

During Fr. García-Herreros’s visits, Carlos had his first confession in decades.

The Second Chance

It was well known that since Lehder’s arrest, the Panamanian dictator, Manuel Noriega, had further extended his assistance to the Medellín narcos, but the Americans didn’t have enough evidence of this to bring him to court. Happily for them, they had someone in prison whose testimony was more than enough to put Noriega on trial. In one of his visits, this was discussed and Fr. García-Herreros encouraged Carlos Lehder to do what all narcos vow to never do: collaborate with the authorities. For the sake of his family’s safety, Lehder needed Pablo Escobar’s blessing before he could cooperate with American prosecutors against Noriega. Fr. García-Herreros became the unlikely go-between, carrying word to Escobar and returning with a promise that Lehder’s family would not be harmed. 
Magnificent Humanity
Get Pope Leo’s Encyclical

It’s important to note that this priest’s relationship with the narcos revolved around the sacraments and leading the narcos out of crime. Even if this didn’t cause a mass conversion amongst the narcos, it did allow for Carlos, the black sheep, to be recovered by Christ.  

Lehder testified against Noriega for five days. His sentence was eventually cut to fifty-five years, and he was moved into the Bureau of Prisons’ witness protection track. He calls Fr. García-Herreros’s intervention the moment that saved him from dying in prison. Shortly after this, Fr. García-Herreros died in 1992. Lehder still speaks of owing him a debt he can never repay.

The Black Sheep

Lehder says his own family had a name for him: “the black sheep.” It’s a phrase he returns to again and again in the book and in interviews, almost as an admission in itself. But Lehder never reaches for the obvious biblical image that phrase references: the parable of the shepherd who leaves ninety-nine sheep safely penned to go looking for the one that wandered off. At this point, I don’t think he needs to be any more explicit. He’s told the story of his own legal, physical, and spiritual rescue openly and enough times for the clear picture to emerge: A man cut off from everyone, in the harshest prison in the American system, was sought out by a priest who crossed an ocean (at the age of eighty-two) to find him and bring him back to Christ. That is, if Lehder wanted to come back. 

Many details about his conversion, atonement, and repentance remain between God and Lehder. But for us outsiders, Lehder’s conversion story is a true-crime and action-film version of the parable of the shepherd and the one lost sheep—black or not. 

What’s Left

Lehder was released in 2020 after thirty-three years behind bars and was deported to Germany, his father’s homeland. He didn’t return to Colombia until March 2025—nearly four decades after he left it in chains—to publish his memoir. He writes that the fortune he once owned is gone, and he now lives a very quiet country life, filling his time reading and walking around the mountains of Colombia where everything started. And he keeps repeating, to anyone who will listen, the same warning: “Everyone who gets involved in drug trafficking ends up either in prison or in the cemetery.” 

One of my personal motivations to write this piece was the fact that on a recent trip to the Colombian coffee axis, I drove multiple times past what once was Lehder’s castle on the hill—a large house visible from a distance. It was once meant to mark the territory but is now in ruins. You’d think it would’ve been demolished by now, but it’s been intentionally left as is as a testament: Crime may buy you a castle on the hill, but it will be worthless anyways. 

Carlos Lehder escaped death in prison and a violent death in the hands of crime by the narrowest and strangest of margins. The sentence meant to take everything from him became the reason he, the black sheep, survived long enough to return—return to his family, to the country he loved, and return to Him.
